title: React Performance and Web Accessibility
description: Measure before optimizing, understand memoization and code splitting, and apply semantic and keyboard-friendly accessibility patterns to real interfaces.
learningOutcomes: Explain why performance optimization should start with evidence and profiling.
Distinguish React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback and know when they are unnecessary.
Use lazy loading and Suspense to defer large code that is not needed immediately.
Build interfaces with semantic elements, accessible names, keyboard operation, and visible focus.
Explain contrast, reduced-motion preferences, and status announcements.
Audit a React screen for performance and accessibility and record before/after evidence.
Choose contextual image alternatives and expose accessible names and toggle state for icon-only controls.

blocks.text: Performance is a user-experience property, not a contest to use the most memoization Hooks. Start with an observed problem and a repeatable scenario: a slow page load, excessive renders, a large bundle, a long main-thread task, or a sluggish interaction. Browser DevTools and React Profiler help locate the expensive work. Optimize a measured bottleneck and measure again; an optimization that adds complexity without improving the delay is not a win.
React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback solve different problems

React.memo can skip rendering a component when its props compare equal. useMemo can reuse a calculation result while its dependencies remain unchanged, and useCallback can reuse a function identity under the same dependency rule. These are performance optimizations, not correctness guarantees. They are helpful when they avoid costly repeated work or keep references stable for a memoized child. They are not automatically useful for every value or callback.

steps.title: Memoize a child only if skipping its renders helps
steps.explanation: memo may skip ProductRow's render when props compare equal. This matters only if it avoids meaningful repeated work in the actual application; it does not make the component correct by itself.

steps.title: Cache filtering while its inputs are stable
steps.explanation: useMemo reuses the filtered array while products and query retain the same dependencies. If filtering is cheap or products is recreated every render, the benefit may be negligible.

steps.title: Keep a callback identity stable for a consumer
steps.explanation: useCallback preserves the function identity while its dependency list remains stable. That can help the memoized child; elsewhere it may be unnecessary.

steps.title: Retain stable list identity
steps.explanation: key identifies a product across list changes. Memoization never removes the need for correct, stable keys.

blocks.title: Memoization is not a correctness fix
blocks.text: Wrong dependencies, mutated state, or unstable keys can still cause bugs. Fix the data model and measure the bottleneck first. Incorrect dependencies can preserve stale results; memoized values are not a substitute for state or effects.
Defer code the user does not need yet

Dynamic import allows a bundler to put code in a separate chunk that loads later. React.lazy loads a component when it is first rendered, and Suspense displays fallback UI while it loads. This can help with large, infrequently visited routes or tools. Splitting every tiny component can add overhead and make the code harder to follow. Also consider what users see if a chunk fails to load.

blocks.text: Use the element that matches the interaction: a button for an action, an anchor for navigation, a label for a form control, and headings for document structure. Native elements provide roles, keyboard activation, and focus behavior that a clickable div does not. ARIA can add an accessible name or state when needed, but it does not automatically implement missing keyboard interactions or turn a semantically wrong control into a correct one.

A page should work with a keyboard: Tab order should be understandable, focus should remain visible, and dialogs should manage focus intentionally. Avoid positive tabindex values that create a separate artificial order. When an action opens a dialog, decide where focus moves; when the dialog closes, return focus to a sensible trigger. Use the browser's native interactions where possible instead of recreating them.
Check contrast, reduced motion, and status announcements

Do not communicate important meaning through color alone. Check text and control contrast in every theme and state. Respect prefers-reduced-motion for nonessential animation. For a dynamic message such as “Changes saved,” use an appropriate status/live-region pattern when assistive technology needs to hear the update; avoid making the entire page a live region.

blocks.caption: Expose a concise status message

Review heading order, accessible names, field labels, error descriptions, and status messages.
Inspect contrast for normal text, controls, focus, disabled states, and dark mode.

Use automated checks as a signal, then manually test real workflows and assistive-technology output.

blocks.text: An image needs an alternative that preserves the information a learner would otherwise miss. If the image adds meaningful information—such as a chart trend, product color, or diagram relationship—write a concise description of that information. If it is purely decorative or repeats the adjacent text, use alt="" so assistive technology can skip it. Do not omit the alt attribute: an empty alternative is an intentional decision, while a missing one may expose a filename or an unhelpful fallback. For an icon-only control, give the control an accessible name and expose toggle state; the glyph itself is not a reliable label.

steps.title: Decide whether the image adds information
steps.explanation: imageAlt is content data: use a useful concise description when the image communicates something not available in nearby text. Use an empty string only when the image is decorative or entirely redundant; do not describe every visual detail.

steps.title: Give the icon button a stable accessible name
steps.explanation: The heart glyph is visual, so aria-label names the control in context. aria-pressed exposes its on/off state to assistive technology. Keep the toggle's name stable while its pressed state changes.

blocks.prompt: A product card shows a photo that only repeats the product name already written in its heading. Which image alternative is usually appropriate?

options.text: Use alt="" because this instance is decorative/redundant
options.feedback: An explicit empty alternative lets assistive technology skip an image that adds no new information.

options.text: Omit alt so the browser can infer the best description
options.feedback: Missing alt is not the same as a deliberate empty alternative and can produce an unhelpful fallback.
This adds no useful information and forces the user to hear an irrelevant description.

options.text: Copy the entire product-card text into alt
options.feedback: Repeating adjacent content creates redundant announcements; describe only information the image uniquely contributes.

blocks.explanation: Choose alternative text based on the image's purpose in context. Empty alt is intentional for decorative/redundant images; informative images need a concise equivalent.

blocks.title: Repair image alternatives and a favorite control
blocks.context: Improve an existing product card so a screen-reader user receives useful image information and can understand and operate the favorite toggle.
instructions: Inspect whether the product image adds information beyond the visible product name; choose a concise description or an intentional empty alternative.
Replace the clickable div with a native button and make its purpose clear without relying on the heart glyph.
Expose the favorite toggle state programmatically and keep the control's accessible name stable across state changes.
Test the control with Tab, Space/Enter, and the browser accessibility tree or a screen reader.
requirements: Every informative image has a concise contextual alternative; decorative/redundant images use alt="".
No image relies on a missing alt attribute or a filename fallback.
The favorite action is a native keyboard-operable button with an accessible name.
The toggle state is exposed with aria-pressed and changes with application state.
The test notes describe the observed name, pressed state, and keyboard behavior.
hints: An empty alt string is correct for a decorative image; do not omit the attribute.
For a toggle button, a stable name such as “Favorite {product.name}” plus aria-pressed communicates purpose and state.
Use the accessibility tree to inspect the computed role, name, and pressed state; then operate it without a mouse.
successCriteria: The image alternative matches the image's purpose in context.
The action is announced as a button with a contextual name.
Pressed/unpressed state is perceivable and updates after activation.
Keyboard activation works and focus remains visible.

blocks.prompt: What is the best first step when a React page seems slow?

options.text: Measure a representative slow scenario and identify the bottleneck
options.feedback: Profiling identifies the work responsible for the delay before more complexity is added.
Memoization may not affect the actual bottleneck and can complicate code.
Stable callbacks matter only for particular reference-sensitive cases.

options.text: Split every component into a separate chunk
options.feedback: Excessive code splitting adds overhead and is not a replacement for measurement.

blocks.explanation: Find and measure the actual bottleneck before choosing an optimization.

blocks.prompt: ARIA on a clickable div automatically gives it the keyboard behavior of a native button.

options.feedback: ARIA can expose semantics but does not automatically implement button keyboard activation or focus behavior.
Prefer native controls; custom controls need correct keyboard, focus, and activation behavior of their own.

blocks.explanation: Semantics and interaction behavior are related but distinct. Native HTML provides important behavior by default.

blocks.prompt: Which are reasonable performance or accessibility practices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use React Profiler or browser tools to find expensive work
options.feedback: Profiling helps prioritize changes against measured problems.

options.text: Use useMemo when caching a calculation has a meaningful benefit
options.feedback: Memoization has costs and should be justified by a real performance or reference-stability need.

options.text: Use color alone as the only indication of an error
options.feedback: Important error meaning must also be communicated through text or semantics.

options.text: Support keyboard operation and visible focus
options.feedback: Keyboard operation and visible focus are essential accessible interaction behaviors.

blocks.explanation: Combine evidence-based optimization with accessibility built into normal interaction patterns.

blocks.text: Deep dive: measure bottlenecks first, preserve keyboard behavior

Performance work should follow evidence. A slow page may be waiting on network resources, parsing/executing a large JavaScript bundle, rendering an expensive subtree, decoding images, or blocking the main thread. `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` only address some render-related costs and can add complexity; they do not fix slow APIs or oversized assets. Accessibility is also behavior: a menu that looks right but cannot be opened, operated and closed with a keyboard is incomplete.

steps.title: Keep the simple derived list readable
steps.explanation: Filtering from current props/state is derived data and does not need its own state plus Effect. For ordinary list sizes, this straightforward code may be fast enough.

steps.title: Use stable keys and semantic navigation
steps.explanation: Stable product IDs preserve item identity, and real links support keyboard use, open-in-new-tab and copy-link behavior that a clickable div would need to recreate.

steps.title: Measure before memoizing
steps.explanation: Use React Profiler and browser performance/network tools to identify the actual bottleneck. Add memoization only when repeated work is measurable and its comparison/maintenance cost makes sense.

items: Check the full user path with keyboard only: Tab/Shift+Tab, Enter/Space, Escape where appropriate, visible focus, and a sensible focus destination after closing overlays.
Use native controls and semantic links/buttons first; ARIA supplements semantics but does not supply keyboard behavior automatically.
Accessible controls need a programmatic name. Icon-only buttons require a text alternative such as an accessible label; labels should describe the action rather than repeat a decorative icon name.
Do not remove focus outlines without replacing them with a clearly visible focus style. Do not convey selected/error/success state by color alone.
For performance, inspect network waterfalls, bundle chunks and main-thread traces before deciding between code splitting, asset optimization or React memoization.

blocks.title: Memoization is an optimization, not a correctness guarantee
blocks.text: A memoized component can still render because its own state or consumed Context changes. `useMemo` and `useCallback` also have comparison and mental overhead. First simplify data flow and measure; keep an optimization when profiling shows it helps the real interaction.

blocks.prompt: A product page is slow because it downloads and parses a very large initial bundle. Which investigation or fix should generally come before adding useCallback to many handlers?

options.text: Profile network and bundle chunks, then consider route-level code splitting or asset reduction
options.feedback: This matches the suspected cost. Callback identity does not reduce the bytes or parse work in the initial bundle.

options.text: Wrap every component in React.memo without measuring
options.feedback: Memoization targets some rendering costs, not download or JavaScript parse cost.
That harms keyboard navigation and does not address performance.

options.text: Replace every button with a clickable div
options.feedback: It removes native semantics without reducing the underlying bundle or execution bottleneck.

blocks.explanation: Match the optimization to the measured bottleneck and preserve semantic interaction behavior.
